The transport credential is the EXPECTED REMOTE TRANSPORT PEER AUTHENTICATOR, established outside rendezvous. In the first concrete profile it is the remote peer's 32-byte WireGuard public key.
R0.6 already separated these experimentally, and R0.9 reuses that separation rather than inventing another credential model:

blocks.text:
NodeId                 semantic identity
WireGuard public key   transport credential
underlay endpoint      location

spans.text: No new cryptosystem and no crypto dependency.
The local private key stays where it already is — in the kernel's WireGuard implementation.
never holds it, never receives candidate peer keys from a directory, and never changes which key is expected.
WireGuard fits the theorem unusually well, because its own roaming rule points the same direction the contract does: a peer's endpoint is updated from the outer source address of a packet that
. Authentication may update location; location never creates authentication.
R0.9 does not own key rotation
R0.6 proved the transport key can rotate while the NodeId does not change. So rotation is somebody else's job.
trusted expectation, supplied by an outside configuration or key-management path.
If that expectation goes stale, connection fails. That is an availability loss, and it is not permission for the rendezvous service to supply a replacement credential.
This is the Tailnet-Lock lesson in miniature: an untrusted coordination plane must not be able to substitute the keys that decide who participates.

blocks.text:
connect(PeerExpectation, EndpointCandidate) -> Result<ValidatedPeerSession>

    1  retarget the ALREADY-EXISTING transport peer at this candidate address
       (update-existing-only; never create, never re-key)
    2  transport authentication                      -- fails => stop
    3  exact-datagram parse of the peer's frame      -- a tail => stop
    4  expected NodeId comparison, over DECODED BYTES -- differs => stop
    5  ValidatedPeerSession

spans.text: Each step's refusal is distinguishable from the others. A control that cannot tell "the network was down" from "the peer failed to authenticate" is measuring a proxy, and this project has lost rounds to exactly that.
Every equality in step 4 is over decoded bytes.
R0.6's version compared 64 hexadecimal characters against 44 base64 characters and therefore could never fire.
5. What the layers may not do to each other

spans.text: Four independent claims, four independent controls. Deriving any one from another is the defect.
